definition: Earnings per share (EPS) is calculated as a company's net profit divided by the number of outstanding shares of its common stock. It is a widely used metric for estimating corporate value.
explanation: EPS is the single most-watched number every earnings season. A rising EPS means the company is becoming more profitable per share you own. At QuantEarningsPro, EPS history — how consistently a company beats, meets, or misses expectations — is one of the core inputs that drives every stock's composite score. See how we score it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: An EPS surprise occurs when the reported earnings per share differ from the analyst consensus estimate. A positive surprise (beat) means actual EPS exceeded expectations; a negative surprise (miss) means it fell short.
explanation: Markets don't just react to whether a company made money — they react to whether it made more or less than expected. Stocks with consistent positive EPS surprises tend to outperform over time. QuantEarningsPro tracks the full surprise history for every covered ticker and weights it directly in the composite score — explore it on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: The price-to-earnings ratio (P/E ratio) is the ratio of a company's share price to its earnings per share. It is calculated by dividing the current stock price by the EPS.
explanation: P/E tells you how much investors are willing to pay for every dollar of earnings. A high P/E can signal expected growth — or overvaluation. QuantEarningsPro incorporates P/E relative to sector peers into the fundamental sub-score so you can quickly identify premium and discount situations. Try filtering by valuation in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Revenue (also called net sales or turnover) is the total amount of income generated by the sale of goods or services related to the company's primary operations.
explanation: Revenue is the top line — the total money flowing into a business before any costs are subtracted. A company growing both revenue and earnings is on solid footing; growing earnings while revenue shrinks may be cutting costs unsustainably. QuantEarningsPro monitors revenue trends as part of the fundamental scoring layer — view it for any stock in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: EBITDA stands for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization. It is a measure of a company's overall financial performance and is used as an alternative to net income in some circumstances.
explanation: EBITDA strips out financing decisions and accounting choices to show you how much cash a business generates from core operations — the preferred profitability metric for comparing companies across different capital structures. QuantEarningsPro includes EBITDA margin trends in the fundamental sub-score. Explore it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: An analyst consensus estimate is the mean or median of earnings forecasts published by equity research analysts covering a given stock. It represents Wall Street's collective expectation for the company's financial results.
explanation: The consensus estimate is the bar a company must clear to 'beat' earnings. Because stocks move on whether they beat or miss this number — not on the raw figure — the consensus is one of the most practically important numbers in investing. QuantEarningsPro shows the current consensus alongside historical surprise data for every ticker on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: Earnings guidance is a report given by a publicly traded company as an estimate of its future earnings. It is usually given at the time of an earnings release and provides forward-looking projections for the next quarter or fiscal year.
explanation: Guidance is often more important than the earnings report itself. When management raises guidance it signals confidence; when they lower it, the market punishes the stock — often more than a single miss would. QuantEarningsPro flags guidance revisions from 8-K filings automatically and alerts you via the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: A whisper number is an unofficial estimate of a company's earnings that circulates among traders and sophisticated investors, often higher or lower than the published analyst consensus.
explanation: Even if a company beats the official analyst consensus, the stock can fall if it misses the whisper number — the informal bar the market has already priced in. Understanding the whisper number explains why markets sometimes react counterintuitively to earnings. QuantEarningsPro's earnings intelligence layer tracks implied expectations to help you navigate this — see it on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: Market capitalization (market cap) is the total market value of a company's outstanding shares of stock. It is calculated by multiplying the current stock price by the total number of outstanding shares.
explanation: Market cap determines whether a stock is large-cap (over $10B), mid-cap ($2–10B), or small-cap (under $2B) — each with different risk and return profiles. QuantEarningsPro lets you filter by market cap range in the screener so you can focus on the size tier that fits your strategy. Filter by size in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Dividend yield is a financial ratio that shows how much a company pays out in dividends each year relative to its stock price. It is expressed as a percentage and calculated by dividing annual dividends per share by the current share price.
explanation: Dividend yield tells income-focused investors how much cash return they receive just from holding the stock. Unusually high yields can signal undervaluation — or an impending dividend cut. QuantEarningsPro's income scoring layer tracks dividend yield alongside payout sustainability for every covered stock. Screen for income opportunities in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: The payout ratio is the proportion of earnings paid out as dividends to shareholders, typically expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing dividends per share by earnings per share.
explanation: A payout ratio below 60% generally indicates a sustainable dividend with room to grow. Above 100%, the company is paying out more than it earns — a dividend cut warning sign. QuantEarningsPro's dividend analytics module tracks payout sustainability alongside yield so income investors can tell the difference between a great deal and a trap. Explore it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Short interest is the total number of shares of a security that have been sold short by investors but have not yet been covered or closed out. It is typically expressed as a percentage of shares outstanding or as a number of days to cover.
explanation: High short interest is a bearish signal — but extreme short interest can also trigger a short squeeze if the stock rises unexpectedly. QuantEarningsPro pulls FINRA short interest data bi-weekly and applies it as a risk-adjustment factor in the composite score, flagging highly-shorted stocks automatically. See it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Days to cover (also called the short interest ratio) is calculated by dividing the total short interest by the average daily trading volume. It represents how many days it would take for all short sellers to close their positions.
explanation: A high days-to-cover reading means short sellers would need many trading days of volume just to buy back their positions — setting the stage for a violent short squeeze if a positive catalyst hits. QuantEarningsPro monitors days-to-cover alongside short interest as part of its risk analytics, surfaced in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Legal insider trading refers to corporate insiders buying or selling shares of their own company's stock, disclosed to the SEC through Form 4 filings within two business days of the transaction.
explanation: When executives buy large amounts of their own company's stock with their personal money, it's one of the strongest bullish signals available — they know the business better than any analyst. QuantEarningsPro monitors SEC EDGAR Form 4 filings automatically and surfaces insider buying clusters as a signal in the composite score. Track insider activity in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Institutional ownership refers to the percentage of a company's shares held by institutional investors such as mutual funds, pension funds, and hedge funds. These positions are disclosed quarterly through SEC Form 13F filings.
explanation: Rising institutional ownership signals growing professional confidence in a stock; sudden reductions across multiple large holders can foreshadow a price decline. QuantEarningsPro automatically parses 13F filings from SEC EDGAR to track institutional flow as part of the scoring model. Follow the smart money in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Implied volatility (IV) is a metric that captures the market's forecast of a likely movement in a security's price. IV is derived from the price of an option and represents the expected annualized standard deviation of price returns over the option's life.
explanation: IV is the options market's forecast of how much a stock will move — in either direction. High IV means options are expensive because the market expects a big move; low IV means options are cheap. QuantEarningsPro computes IV metrics nightly and uses them in the IV Squeeze detector — a tool that identifies when volatility has compressed to levels that historically precede large moves. See it on the QuantEarningsPro IV Squeeze Detector.

definition: An IV Squeeze occurs when a stock's implied volatility falls to unusually low levels relative to its historical range. It signals a period of low expected movement that often precedes a significant price breakout.
explanation: When IV compresses to multi-month lows, options become cheap — at exactly the time when a breakout may be building. QuantEarningsPro's proprietary IV Squeeze score (0–100) quantifies this setup nightly for the top 500 tickers, making it easy to find high-probability setups before the market wakes up. Explore current squeeze setups on the QuantEarningsPro IV Squeeze Detector.

definition: IV crush refers to the rapid decline in implied volatility that typically occurs immediately after a major event such as an earnings release. As the uncertainty resolves, the options market rapidly deflates the premium that had been priced in.
explanation: Even if a stock moves after earnings, IV crush can wipe out an option's value — because you bought at peak IV right before it collapsed. Understanding IV crush is fundamental to any earnings options strategy. QuantEarningsPro's earnings options tools model IV crush risk before you enter a trade. Build smarter earnings strategies with the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: An options chain (or option matrix) is a listing of all available option contracts for a given security, organized by expiration date and strike price. It displays current bid, ask, volume, open interest, and implied volatility for each contract.
explanation: The options chain is the complete menu of available contracts for a stock — where the money is concentrated, how expensive different strikes are, and what expirations traders are focused on. QuantEarningsPro pulls end-of-day options chains for all covered tickers and uses them to compute IV metrics, squeeze scores, and strategy recommendations. View them in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: Open interest is the total number of outstanding options or futures contracts that have not been settled. Unlike volume, open interest counts only open positions that have not been closed, expired, or exercised.
explanation: High open interest at a specific strike shows where the most options money is concentrated — often a magnet for price. Unusual spikes in OI signal where sophisticated traders are positioning ahead of a catalyst. QuantEarningsPro monitors OI changes across covered tickers as part of its options intelligence layer. Explore it with the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: A straddle is an options strategy that involves simultaneously purchasing or selling a call and a put option on the same underlying security, with the same strike price and expiration date.
explanation: A long straddle profits if the stock makes a large move in either direction — you don't need to predict which way, just that it will move significantly. It's a common earnings strategy, but IV crush is the risk if the move is smaller than expected. QuantEarningsPro's earnings strategy library includes pre-built straddle templates with historical performance data. Try it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: A strangle is an options strategy where the investor holds a position in both a call and a put option with different strike prices but the same expiration date and underlying asset.
explanation: Like a straddle, a strangle profits from a big move in either direction — but it's cheaper because the call and put are out-of-the-money. The tradeoff: the stock needs to move even more to be profitable. QuantEarningsPro's earnings strategy templates include strangle setups with implied move data so you can evaluate the risk/reward before earnings. Build it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: An iron condor is an options strategy consisting of two puts and two calls at four different strike prices but the same expiration. It generates a net credit and profits if the underlying stays within a defined range.
explanation: An iron condor bets that a stock won't move dramatically — you collect premium if it stays range-bound. Around earnings, selling an iron condor means betting the move will be smaller than the market expects. QuantEarningsPro's strategy library includes iron condor templates with historical win rate data by implied move percentile. Explore it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: Delta measures the rate of change in an option's price per $1 change in the underlying asset's price. Call options have positive delta (0 to 1); put options have negative delta (−1 to 0).
explanation: Delta tells you how much an option moves when the stock moves $1 — and roughly approximates the probability the option expires in-the-money. QuantEarningsPro calculates all Greeks client-side in real time as you build strategies, so you always know your true directional exposure. See your Greeks live in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: Gamma is the rate of change of an option's delta relative to a $1 move in the underlying asset's price. It measures the curvature of the option's value relative to the underlying price.
explanation: Gamma tells you how fast delta changes as the stock moves. Near-term, at-the-money options have the highest gamma — they react most explosively to stock movement. QuantEarningsPro computes gamma alongside delta, theta, and vega for every strategy so you understand exactly how your position will behave across different stock moves. Build and analyze strategies in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: Theta is the rate of decline in the value of an option due to the passage of time. It represents the daily dollar amount an option loses as it approaches expiration, all else being equal.
explanation: Theta is time decay — the silent cost of holding long options. Every day without the expected move, your option loses value. QuantEarningsPro's strategy builder shows you daily theta decay for any position so you can see exactly what holding cost you're accepting when you plan an earnings trade. Model it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: Vega measures an option's sensitivity to changes in implied volatility. It represents the change in an option's price for every 1-percentage-point change in implied volatility.
explanation: Vega is why options get more expensive when uncertainty rises — and why IV crush hurts long options buyers so much after earnings. Managing vega is critical when positioning around events. QuantEarningsPro displays vega alongside all other Greeks in real time for any strategy, helping you understand exactly how an IV change will affect your P&L. See it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: A volatility surface is a three-dimensional plot of implied volatility across different strike prices and expiration dates for a given underlying asset.
explanation: The volatility surface is a complete map of what the market expects across every strike and expiration — revealing skew, term structure, and overall fear or complacency. QuantEarningsPro's Volatility Surface Explorer lets you view and replay the IV surface before and after earnings events, revealing patterns that inform smarter strategy selection. Explore it on the QuantEarningsPro Volatility Surface Explorer.

definition: The implied move is the expected magnitude of a stock's price change following a binary event (typically earnings), as derived from options pricing. It is calculated by adding the prices of the at-the-money call and put for the nearest expiration after the event.
explanation: The options market votes on how far a stock will move at earnings — the implied move is that vote. Whether the stock actually moves more or less than the implied move is the key question every earnings options trader analyzes. QuantEarningsPro displays the current implied move for every upcoming earnings event and backtests how often stocks have beaten or missed it historically. See it on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: A market regime refers to the prevailing state or environment of the overall stock market at a given time — typically classified as bull market, bear market, correction, or sideways — each characterized by distinct price trends, volatility levels, and investor behavior.
explanation: A stock scoring 7.5 in a bull market is a very different opportunity than the same score during a bear market with an inverted yield curve. QuantEarningsPro runs a dual-layer regime detection engine — price-action based and macro-based — that adjusts how composite scores are weighted depending on the current market environment. Check the current regime reading on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: A bull market is a financial market condition in which prices are rising or are expected to rise. The term most commonly refers to the stock market but applies to any traded asset.
explanation: In a bull market, rising prices create positive momentum, increased confidence, and more willingness to take on risk. QuantEarningsPro's regime detection identifies bull market conditions and automatically shifts scoring weights toward growth and momentum factors — surfacing the stocks best positioned to benefit. Check the current regime on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: A bear market is a condition in which securities prices fall 20% or more from recent highs amid widespread pessimism and negative investor sentiment.
explanation: Bear markets change the rules — strategies that work in bull markets become dangerous. QuantEarningsPro's regime detection adjusts scoring weights during bear markets to prioritize defensive characteristics: strong balance sheets, low leverage, and reliable earnings. The system enters 'max defensive mode' when multiple macro signals align bearishly. Monitor conditions on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The yield curve is a line that plots yields of bonds having equal credit quality but differing maturity dates. The most commonly referenced is the U.S. Treasury yield curve, plotting 3-month, 2-year, 5-year, 10-year, and 30-year Treasury rates.
explanation: The shape of the yield curve reveals economic expectations. An upward slope is healthy; an inverted curve (short rates above long rates) has preceded every U.S. recession since 1955. QuantEarningsPro monitors the 2Y-10Y spread daily as a core input into the macro regime layer — when it inverts, scoring weights shift defensively. Track the current curve on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: A yield curve inversion occurs when short-term Treasury yields rise above long-term yields, resulting in a negative spread. The most closely watched inversion is when the 2-year Treasury yield exceeds the 10-year yield.
explanation: Every U.S. recession since the 1950s has been preceded by a yield curve inversion, with an average lag of 12–18 months. When the curve inverts, QuantEarningsPro's macro regime layer shifts to late-cycle or contraction mode, reducing weight on high-growth, high-beta names and increasing emphasis on quality filters. Monitor the live 2Y-10Y spread on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other banks overnight. It is set by the FOMC of the Federal Reserve and is the primary tool of U.S. monetary policy.
explanation: The Fed Funds Rate is the most important single number in financial markets — it sets the cost of borrowing across the entire economy and directly affects stock valuations, especially high-growth names. QuantEarningsPro ingests rate data from FRED daily and incorporates rate trajectory into macro regime weighting, so your scores already reflect the interest rate environment. See the impact on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the weighted average of prices of a basket of consumer goods and services. It is the main gauge of inflation in the United States.
explanation: High and rising CPI puts pressure on the Fed to raise interest rates, which hurts stocks — especially high-multiple growth names. CPI prints are among the most market-moving economic releases. QuantEarningsPro tracks CPI trend via FRED as a key input into the macro regime classification and economic calendar alerts. See upcoming CPI dates and their market impact on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a leading economic indicator derived from monthly surveys of private sector companies. A PMI above 50 represents expansion; below 50 represents contraction.
explanation: PMI is a leading economic indicator — it tells you what's happening in the economy before official GDP data is published. A falling PMI alongside rising CPI signals stagflation — the most damaging macro condition for equity valuations. QuantEarningsPro uses PMI data from FRED to classify macro regimes and adjust composite score weights accordingly. Track it on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: Credit spreads are the yield difference between a corporate bond and a comparable-maturity U.S. Treasury bond. Widening spreads signal rising default risk; tightening spreads signal confidence.
explanation: Credit spreads are the financial market's fear gauge for the corporate sector. When spreads widen, it typically precedes stock market declines. QuantEarningsPro monitors both investment-grade and high-yield spreads via FRED as macro regime inputs — when spreads blow out, the system shifts scoring weights defensively to protect your portfolio. See the current reading on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is the branch of the Federal Reserve System that determines monetary policy by setting the federal funds rate. It meets eight times per year.
explanation: FOMC meetings are the most market-moving scheduled events in the economic calendar. Rate-sensitive sectors — utilities, REITs, financials — are especially affected in the days surrounding each meeting. QuantEarningsPro's economic calendar flags all eight FOMC meetings annually and applies a rate-sensitive sector warning flag in the week leading up to each decision. See upcoming FOMC dates on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: The Non-Farm Payrolls report measures the change in the number of employed people in the U.S. during the previous month, excluding farm workers. It is released on the first Friday of each month by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
explanation: The jobs report is one of the most watched economic releases in the world — a strong report can push the Fed to keep rates higher; a weak one can signal economic slowdown. QuantEarningsPro's integrated economic calendar includes NFP release dates alongside earnings events so you always see the full event risk picture for the week. Track it on the QuantEarningsPro Earnings Calendar.

definition: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period. It is the broadest measure of economic health.
explanation: Two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth are the informal definition of a recession. QuantEarningsPro ingests GDP data from FRED and uses it to confirm or challenge what leading indicators like PMI and credit spreads have been signaling — completing the macro picture that drives regime classification. See how current GDP fits the overall regime on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months. The informal rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth.
explanation: Recessions aren't just economic events — they're investment events. Different types of stocks behave very differently: consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare tend to hold up; cyclicals, small-caps, and high-leverage companies get hit hardest. QuantEarningsPro's macro regime layer enters 'max defensive mode' when recession signals align, automatically adjusting how every stock in the screener is scored. See your portfolio exposure on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: Stagflation is a macroeconomic condition characterized by slow economic growth, high unemployment, and high inflation occurring simultaneously.
explanation: Stagflation is the worst of both worlds — the Fed can't cut rates to stimulate growth without fueling more inflation. For investors, it particularly damages high-multiple growth stocks and bonds. QuantEarningsPro detects stagflation signals (rising CPI + falling PMI) within the macro regime layer and flags rate-sensitive sectors at elevated risk. Monitor current conditions on the QuantEarningsPro Market Regime Dashboard.

definition: The Sharpe ratio measures the performance of an investment compared to a risk-free asset, after adjusting for risk. It is calculated by subtracting the risk-free rate from the portfolio return and dividing by the standard deviation of excess return.
explanation: Sharpe ratio answers: 'Am I being compensated for the risk I'm taking?' A ratio above 1.0 is generally acceptable; above 2.0 is very good. Two strategies with the same returns but different Sharpe ratios tell very different stories. QuantEarningsPro's backtesting engine reports Sharpe alongside raw returns so you evaluate every strategy on a risk-adjusted basis. Run your own backtest on the QuantEarningsPro Backtesting Engine.

definition: The Sortino ratio is a modification of the Sharpe ratio that uses only downside deviation (the standard deviation of negative returns) rather than total volatility.
explanation: Unlike Sharpe, the Sortino ratio only penalizes downside volatility — because upside volatility isn't a problem. For earnings-event driven strategies that generate lumpy but mostly positive returns, Sortino is often a more relevant metric than Sharpe. QuantEarningsPro's backtesting engine reports Sortino alongside Sharpe, max drawdown, and win rate for complete strategy evaluation. Run your backtest on the QuantEarningsPro Backtesting Engine.

definition: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) is the rate of return required for an investment to grow from its beginning balance to its ending balance, assuming profits were reinvested at the end of each year.
explanation: CAGR is the most honest way to compare strategies across different time periods — it accounts for compounding and smooths out lumpy year-by-year results. QuantEarningsPro's backtesting engine reports CAGR for every tested strategy alongside S&P 500 benchmark comparison so you can see exactly how much alpha the strategy has generated historically. Test it on the QuantEarningsPro Backtesting Engine.

definition: Maximum drawdown (MDD) is the maximum observed loss from a peak to a trough of a portfolio before a new peak is attained. It measures downside risk over a specified period.
explanation: Max drawdown answers: 'What's the worst losing streak this strategy has had?' A strategy with 20% CAGR but a 60% max drawdown may be psychologically impossible to hold through. QuantEarningsPro's backtesting engine reports max drawdown prominently — because a strategy you can't stick with in practice isn't a real strategy. Stress-test your approach on the QuantEarningsPro Backtesting Engine.

definition: Alpha is a measure of an investment's active return relative to a market index or benchmark. Positive alpha means outperformance on a risk-adjusted basis; negative alpha means underperformance.
explanation: Alpha is the holy grail — returns above and beyond what the market gave you for free. QuantEarningsPro's scoring system is designed to identify stocks with the characteristics historically associated with positive alpha: improving earnings momentum, strong technicals, and appropriate valuation relative to the macro regime. See which stocks are generating alpha signals right now in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Beta measures a stock's volatility in relation to the overall market. A beta of 1 means the stock moves in line with the market; above 1 means more volatile; below 1 means less volatile.
explanation: High-beta stocks amplify both gains and losses relative to the market. In a bull regime, high-beta accelerates returns; in a bear regime, it accelerates losses. QuantEarningsPro's regime detection reduces score weighting for high-beta names when macro conditions are bearish, helping you avoid the stocks that hurt most when things go wrong. Screen by beta in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Backtesting is the process of testing a trading strategy against historical data to evaluate how it would have performed in the past.
explanation: Backtesting lets you stress-test a strategy before risking real money. QuantEarningsPro's backtesting engine is regime-aware — it shows you how a strategy performs across different market environments, not just in aggregate. You can backtest both fundamental scoring strategies and earnings-event options strategies. Start testing on the QuantEarningsPro Backtesting Engine.

definition: A Monte Carlo simulation uses random sampling to estimate the probability of different outcomes in a process that cannot easily be predicted due to random variables. In investing, it models the range of possible portfolio or strategy outcomes.
explanation: Monte Carlo takes 'what if' analysis to the next level — instead of one outcome, it runs thousands of randomized scenarios to generate a probability-weighted distribution of results. QuantEarningsPro's earnings scenario engine runs Monte Carlo simulations directly in your browser for any options strategy, showing you the full range of possible P&L outcomes before you place a trade. Try it in the QuantEarningsPro Options Strategy Builder.

definition: SHAP is a game theory-based approach to explain the output of any machine learning model. It assigns each input feature an importance value showing how much it contributed to a specific prediction.
explanation: SHAP solves the AI black-box problem. When QuantEarningsPro's earnings prediction model assigns a stock a 70% probability of a large post-earnings move, SHAP explains exactly why: which factors drove that prediction and by how much. Every AI-generated prediction on the platform comes with SHAP feature attributions so you can understand and evaluate the model's reasoning. See it in action on the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Sector rotation is an investment strategy involving moving money from one industry sector to another in anticipation of the next stage of the economic cycle.
explanation: Sector rotation is how institutional money moves through the market cycle — technology leads in early bull markets; energy and materials in mid-cycle; utilities and healthcare in late-cycle and recession. QuantEarningsPro's sector rotation heatmaps show which GICS sectors currently have the highest average composite scores, helping you identify where the next leadership shift may be heading. Explore it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: The Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) is an industry taxonomy developed by MSCI and S&P Global. It consists of 11 sectors, 25 industry groups, 74 industries, and 163 sub-industries.
explanation: GICS is the standard framework for classifying stocks by industry. QuantEarningsPro uses GICS classifications to aggregate scores by sector, power the sector rotation heatmaps, and apply sector-relative valuation scoring so you're always comparing a stock to the right peer group. Filter by GICS sector in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a pooled investment security that trades on a stock exchange throughout the day at market-determined prices, typically tracking an index, sector, commodity, or other asset.
explanation: ETFs combine the diversification of a mutual fund with the trading flexibility of a stock. For options traders, ETFs like SPY, QQQ, and IWM offer the most liquid options markets in existence. QuantEarningsPro's Phase 5 ETF analytics suite brings full scoring, screening, and options strategy tools to the U.S.-listed ETF universe. See what's coming on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: Net asset value (NAV) is the value per share of a mutual fund or ETF, calculated as the total value of the fund's underlying holdings minus liabilities, divided by shares outstanding.
explanation: NAV is what an ETF is 'really worth' based on its holdings. When an ETF trades at a premium to NAV, you're paying more than its underlying assets are worth; at a discount, you're getting a bargain. QuantEarningsPro's upcoming ETF analytics suite tracks premium/discount to NAV for every covered ETF as a core scoring factor. Learn more about our ETF coverage on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: The expense ratio is the annual fee a fund charges its shareholders, expressed as a percentage of percentage of average assets under management. It covers operating costs including management fees and administrative expenses.
explanation: Expense ratio is the most predictive factor in long-term fund performance — lower costs directly translate to better returns. An ETF charging 0.03% vs. one at 0.75% may seem minor, but compounded over 20 years the difference is enormous. QuantEarningsPro's ETF scoring engine makes expense ratio a primary scoring factor so cost-efficient funds rise to the top. Explore our ETF scoring approach on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: Tracking error is the divergence between the price behavior of a portfolio (typically an index ETF) and the price behavior of its benchmark index, measured as the standard deviation of return differences.
explanation: For an index ETF, tracking error tells you how closely the fund actually follows its benchmark. A high tracking error means you're not getting the index return you're paying for. QuantEarningsPro's ETF scoring engine includes tracking error as a scoring factor — because passive investors deserve funds that actually track their index. Learn more on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: Contango is a situation where the futures price of a commodity is higher than the expected spot price at contract maturity. In contango, futures curves slope upward — contracts further out are priced higher than near-term contracts.
explanation: Contango is the silent tax on commodity ETF investors. When an ETF rolls expiring contracts into the next month, it sells the cheap near-term contract and buys the more expensive future-dated one — eroding returns over time even if spot prices are flat. QuantEarningsPro's Phase 7 commodity analytics engine tracks term structure and roll yield for all covered commodity markets. Preview it on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: Backwardation is a market condition where near-term futures contracts trade at a premium to longer-dated contracts — the opposite of contango. It often signals near-term supply tightness or strong immediate demand.
explanation: Backwardation is positive for commodity ETF investors — the ETF earns a roll yield when it sells the expensive near-term contract and buys the cheaper future-dated one. Markets in backwardation often signal fundamental bullishness: demand is outpacing supply right now. QuantEarningsPro's commodity term structure engine tracks backwardation/contango regime for energy, metals, and agricultural futures. See it on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: The Commitments of Traders (COT) report is a weekly CFTC publication showing aggregate positions of different groups of traders — commercial hedgers, large speculators, and small speculators — across U.S. futures and options markets.
explanation: The COT report is one of the most underutilized signals in investing. When commercial hedgers — the producers and consumers with real exposure — are at historically extreme net-long positions while speculators are heavily short, it often precedes a price reversal. QuantEarningsPro's Phase 7 commodity engine processes weekly CFTC data to surface these positioning extremes as actionable signals. Learn more on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: Assets under management (AUM) refers to the total market value of investments that a financial institution manages on behalf of clients. For ETFs and mutual funds, AUM is the total value of the fund's holdings.
explanation: AUM is a measure of scale and investor confidence. For ETFs, larger AUM means better liquidity and tighter spreads. For mutual funds, rising AUM signals net inflows — investors adding money — while falling AUM can force managers to sell holdings at inopportune times. QuantEarningsPro tracks AUM flow trends from SEC N-PORT filings as a leading sentiment indicator. Explore it on the QuantEarningsPro Platform Roadmap.

definition: A moving average (MA) smooths out price data by creating a constantly updated average price over a specified period. Common periods are 20, 50, and 200 days. The simple moving average (SMA) weights all periods equally; the exponential moving average (EMA) weights recent prices more heavily.
explanation: Moving averages cut through daily price noise to reveal the underlying trend. The 200-day MA is the most widely watched: stocks above it are generally in uptrends; below it, downtrends. QuantEarningsPro incorporates multiple moving average signals into the technical sub-score for every stock, weighting momentum and trend direction in the composite. See moving average signals in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: The Relative Strength Index (RSI) is a momentum oscillator measuring the speed and change of price movements on a scale of 0 to 100. RSI above 70 indicates overbought conditions; below 30 indicates oversold conditions.
explanation: RSI tells you how aggressively a stock has been bought or sold relative to its recent history. An overbought RSI heading into earnings is a caution signal; an oversold RSI on a fundamentally strong stock can be an opportunity. QuantEarningsPro incorporates RSI as part of the technical sub-score in the composite rating for every covered stock. Find oversold setups in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: MACD is a trend-following momentum indicator showing the relationship between two exponential moving averages (typically 12-day and 26-day) of a security's price. Crossovers of the MACD line and signal line are used as trading signals.
explanation: MACD captures both trend and momentum in one indicator. A shrinking histogram on a declining stock can be an early warning of a reversal. QuantEarningsPro uses MACD signal direction as one of several technical inputs that contribute to the momentum component of every stock's composite score. Track technical signals across the market in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Bollinger Bands characterize prices and volatility using a simple moving average (middle band) and two standard deviation bands above and below it. The bands expand during high volatility and contract during low volatility.
explanation: When Bollinger Bands squeeze tight, it signals an impending breakout — a pattern closely related to the IV Squeeze in options markets. QuantEarningsPro uses Bollinger Band width as a volatility signal in the technical scoring layer, helping identify stocks where a significant move is building. Find tight-band setups in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: Momentum in investing refers to the tendency for securities that have performed well recently to continue performing well in the near future, and vice versa. It is typically measured as the rate of price change over 1, 3, 6, or 12 months.
explanation: Momentum is one of the most robust and well-documented factors in academic finance — stocks that have outperformed recently tend to continue outperforming over the next 3–12 months. QuantEarningsPro incorporates multi-period price momentum as a key technical sub-score component in the composite rating. Screen for high-momentum stocks on the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: A Registered Investment Advisor (RIA) is a person or firm that advises clients on securities investments and manages portfolios. RIAs are registered with the SEC or state regulators and are held to a fiduciary standard — legally required to act in clients' best interests.
explanation: RIAs are fiduciaries — a higher legal standard than broker-dealers. Independent RIAs managing their own research workflow are the primary professional users QuantEarningsPro is built for: professionals who need Bloomberg-caliber analytics at a fraction of the $2,665/month Bloomberg price tag. See how QuantEarningsPro serves independent advisors on the QuantEarningsPro Advisor Plan page.

definition: EDGAR (Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval) is the SEC's online database of filings submitted by public companies, providing free public access to all SEC filings including 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, Form 4, and 13F reports.
explanation: EDGAR is one of the most valuable free resources for investors — a complete database of everything public companies are legally required to disclose. QuantEarningsPro mines EDGAR continuously for earnings filings, material event disclosures, insider transactions, and institutional holdings — delivering the intelligence from thousands of filings directly inside the platform so you never have to dig manually. See it in action on the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: A 10-K is a comprehensive annual report required by the SEC for all publicly traded companies. It includes audited financial statements, business description, risk factors, and management's discussion and analysis (MD&A).
explanation: The 10-K is the most complete financial disclosure a public company makes — written for investors and regulators, not for marketing. QuantEarningsPro's NLP scoring engine reads 10-K management discussion sections automatically, extracting sentiment signals that feed into the composite score. You get the intelligence from thousands of annual reports without reading a single one. Explore it in the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: A 10-Q is a quarterly report public companies file with the SEC. It includes unaudited financial statements and management commentary on the company's financial position between annual reports.
explanation: The 10-Q is the quarterly pulse check — often containing updated risk disclosures and management commentary that signals whether business conditions are improving or deteriorating. QuantEarningsPro's SEC filing NLP engine reads 10-Q filings as they arrive and updates sentiment scores within the composite rating. Stay ahead of changes on the QuantEarningsPro Stock Screener.

definition: An 8-K is a report public companies must file with the SEC to announce major events shareholders should know about — including earnings announcements, executive changes, acquisitions, guidance revisions, and other material events.
explanation: The 8-K is the market's breaking news wire for public companies — when something material happens, it must be filed within 4 business days. QuantEarningsPro monitors 8-K filings in near real-time and generates alerts on material events for your watched tickers: guidance revisions, dilutive offerings, restatements, and executive changes.
